### Russell Brand, One Week After Sentence: The Prison Message Under Investigation, the Sentence in British Numbers, and the Martyr Argument

Filed as: Special Report — Filed Outside the Watches · 2026-11-16T12:45:00-05:00 · https://objectivedailynews.com/special-reports/2026-11-16-russell-brand-sentence.html

Special Report

 The Case File, Continued—One Week On, and the Sentence in Its Own System’s Numbers

 Objective

 Russell Brand, One Week After Sentence: The Prison Message Under Investigation, the Sentence in British Numbers, and the Martyr Argument — Special Report

 On Sunday, November 15, Laura Gallacher read a message from her husband on the couple’s YouTube programme Sunday Service: “As you know, I am not guilty for the offences I have been jailed for, so something strange is happening.” On Monday, November 16, Downing Street said the message was “clearly appalling” and is being urgently investigated as a possible breach of the prison rules, which bar prisoners from making statements that cause distress to victims and provide that a prisoner breaks the rules by giving comments to a family member knowing they will be published. Russell Brand, 51, is one week into a sentence of 10 years and 6 months, passed at Southwark Crown Court on Monday, November 9, 2026, on a jury’s unanimous verdicts of November 5: one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault, offences of 2004 to 2009, with acquittals on three further counts. This report, the follow-up to the desk’s Special Report of November 9, which filed the charges, the verdicts, and the judge’s reasons in full, files Monday’s development and the rules framework it turns on; measures the sentence against the British baselines—the statutory definition, the Sentencing Council’s guideline, and the national distribution of rape sentences; sets out the four structural differences that would have governed the same facts in an American courtroom; prints both camps’ exhibits on the targeting question, including the precedent line of establishment figures the same system prosecuted; and closes with the martyrdom reaction in its three attributed positions. The desk weighs none of the contested claims; where a claim can be checked against the record, the record is printed.

 By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 1245 ET, Monday, November 16, 2026.

The Week in Brief

The new proceeding is disciplinary, and it opened on Monday. The Ministry of Justice is investigating whether Brand broke the prison rules by sending the message his wife broadcast. No finding has been announced, and Brand’s side has made no public response to the investigation in the record the desk found. The desk files the two things the government produced on Monday separately below: the rules as the Prison Rules 1999 write them, and the reaction as the officials gave it.

The rest of the week’s record is movement inside the sentence and pressure outside it. Brand was transferred on Friday, November 13, from HMP Wandsworth, a category B prison, to HMP Littlehey, a category C prison in Cambridgeshire—reported by tabloid and aggregator sources and confirmed by his own message, which names the prison. On November 12, his official account on X shared a supporter petition, “Free Russell Brand,” carrying five demands; the petition states that it is independent and not authorised by Brand or his lawyers. On November 12 and 13, The Times and The Sunday Times published accounts from six further women, incidents alleged from 2005 to 2015, withheld until the trial ended; three feature in a Netflix documentary, Russell Brand: Open Secret, released Friday, November 13. The accounts are journalism, untested in any court; the Metropolitan Police says several people contacted it during and after the trial and officers are reviewing the material, and the two further rape investigations already on file remain with the Crown Prosecution Service, undecided. No appeal had been filed in any reporting the desk found as of Monday; the windows run to December 3 for conviction and December 7 for sentence.

The baselines this report measures against are the system’s own. The offence is defined by the Sexual Offences Act 2003; the sentence was built inside the Sentencing Council’s guideline for rape, whose full range runs from 4 to 19 years; and the Sentencing Academy’s snapshot of the Ministry of Justice’s 2025 figures records 1,602 rape convictions in the year, the most frequent sentence band at 10 to 15 years, and an average custodial term of almost 11 years. Against those instruments—and against the funnel through which recorded rapes pass, in which about 3 in 100 recorded offences had resulted in a charge on the latest published count—the sentence is placed in Section 2, the American comparison in Section 3, and the argument about why this defendant, in Sections 4 and 5.

1. Monday’s Development: A Message From HMP Littlehey, and the Rules It Is Being Tested Against

The message was read on Sunday, November 15, in the couple’s weekly programme. Gallacher told viewers, “Russell has asked me to read something to you,” and read from a notebook, as carried in the transcripts of the broadcast: “Beloved brothers and sisters in Christ, God bless you for your support. As you know, I am not guilty for the offences I have been jailed for, so something strange is happening. The good news is that Christ is with us when we choose him, and I do. I am incarcerated in HMP Littlehey, little as in small, and hey as in hey, I’m in the biggest sex offenders’ prison in Europe.” Of the other prisoners he wrote that he was in no position to judge anyone—“the ones that are, they are people that Christ died to save, like you and me”—and the message closed: “Please support my treasured wife and family. I feel your prayers, your brother in Christ. Russell.” The Sun counted more than 150,000 views of the episode by Monday. The channel’s scale is the factual reason a prison message becomes a public event: The Observer counted, in October 2026, 6.62 million subscribers on YouTube, 2.2 million followers on Rumble, and 4.9 million on Instagram, and reporting this month puts his following on X above 10 million.

The government answered on Monday, November 16, in two registers, and the desk keeps them apart. The first register is administrative. The Prime Minister’s official spokesman, as carried by the Press Association: “This is clearly appalling, and is being urgently investigated. We expect action to be taken if he’s found to have broken the rules. Prisoners are strictly banned from making statements that cause distress to victims, and speaking to the media is only permitted in exceptional circumstances. Prisoners cannot get around these rules by having someone else publish their comments.” The Press Association adds the operative understanding: a prisoner will be deemed to have broken the rules if he provides comments to a family member that he knows will be published. The second register is ministerial reaction, attributed as such. The Foreign Secretary, Ed Miliband, told Sky News: “His crimes are heinous and awful. I think it’s revolting, by the way, that he shows no remorse today in his comments. No remorse, no sympathy for the victims. Just disgusting comments.” Miliband repeated his apology for interviewing Brand on his programme in 2015. Andrea Simon, the Victims’ Commissioner for London, told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme that the continued claims of innocence would “certainly retraumatise his victims.” Separately, The Times reported on Monday that the Justice Secretary, Alex Norris, has written to the Bar Standards Board warning that it is unacceptable for barristers to perpetuate myths about rape victims in court—a government intervention on the trial’s other flank, filed here as reported.

The rules framework is statute and standing order, and it is older than this case. The Prison Act 1952, section 47, empowers the Secretary of State to make rules for the regulation, discipline, and control of prisoners; the Prison Rules 1999 are those rules. Rule 34(1) provides that a prisoner shall not communicate with any person outside the prison except with the leave of the Secretary of State or as a privilege under rule 8, the privileges system; rule 34(2) permits restrictions on communications on stated grounds, including the protection of the rights and freedoms of any person, and correspondence and calls may be read and monitored. The publication bar sits in the standing orders reproduced in the courts’ case law: a prisoner’s general correspondence may not contain material intended for publication, or likely to be published, if it is about the inmate’s crime or past offences. That bar was tested by the murderer Dennis Nilsen, who sought to publish an autobiography, and upheld through the Court of Appeal in 2004: the judgment records both the rule and the governor’s power to examine material intended for publication. The question the investigation must answer is therefore narrow: whether a message handed to a wife for broadcast is the prisoner’s own publication by another hand, which the spokesman’s formulation and the Press Association’s understanding both say the rules treat it as.

If a breach is found, the ladder of consequences is also written down. Disciplinary charges are heard as adjudications. Under rule 55, a governor who finds a prisoner guilty may impose a caution; forfeiture of the rule 8 privileges for up to 42 days; exclusion from associated work; stoppage of earnings; cellular confinement for up to 21 days; or removal from the prisoner’s wing for 28 days. Where a charge is serious enough that additional days might be awarded, rule 53A sends it to an independent adjudicator—a district judge—who under rule 55A may add up to 42 days to the time served. Recategorisation and transfer sit outside the adjudication as administrative measures. The Press Association’s reporting carries the nearest precedent: in 2022 the prisoner Charles Bronson reportedly received a 28-day restriction on his telephone use after sending an audio message about his parole bid to Sky News, having, he said, been told he had breached the rules by not seeking the governor’s permission. The investigation is open; what it finds, and what follows, are future facts.

2. The Sentence in British Numbers: The Definition, the Guideline, and the Distribution

The offence Brand was convicted of is defined by section 1 of the Sexual Offences Act 2003, and the definition is the first baseline. A person commits rape if he intentionally penetrates the vagina, anus, or mouth of another person with his penis, that person does not consent to the penetration, and he does not reasonably believe that she consents. Consent, under section 74, means a person “agrees by choice, and has the freedom and capacity to make that choice.” The maximum sentence is life imprisonment. No element of violence, of a weapon, of injury, or of a stranger is in the definition; the crime is penetration without consent, and in count 6 the jury’s finding, as the judge recorded it, was that an encounter which began with consent continued after the condom was removed and after two loud requests to stop. That is the whole of the actus reus the Crown had to prove, and it is why a case can turn, as this one did, on testimony about consent rather than on forensic evidence of force.

The sentence was built inside a published grid. The Sentencing Council’s guideline for rape sets an offence range of 4 to 19 years. Mr Justice Bennathan placed the rape in category 2B—harm category 2, culpability B—starting point 8 years, range 7 to 9. The prosecution had sought category 1, starting point 12 years, range 10 to 15; the judge refused it, refused also to treat Brand’s fame as an abuse of trust or as an overarching aggravating factor, raised the term to the top of the 2B range for the condom’s removal and its consequences, and took one year off for the mitigation he accepted: no significant previous convictions, 17 years since the last offence, the addiction-recovery work a witness called particularly impressive, and the impact on Brand’s children. Nine years is therefore two things at once, and the desk prints both: the ceiling of the category the judge chose, and a figure below the national average for the offence, which is computed across every category including the stranger, weapon, and campaign cases of category 1. The three sexual assaults drew 9, 18, and 8 months, concurrent with each other and consecutive to the rape; the guideline range for sexual assault runs from a community order to 7 years, so those terms sit in the lower half of their own grid.

The national distribution, from the Sentencing Academy’s snapshot of the Ministry of Justice’s figures for sentences imposed in 2025, is the second baseline. There were 1,602 convictions for rape in the year. The most frequent sentence band was 10 to 15 years, at 26 per cent of immediate custodial sentences; about 21 per cent received more than 15 years; by the Academy’s own figures, some 47 per cent of rape sentences were 10 years or more. The average custodial sentence length for rape has risen from about 8 years in 2010 to almost 11 years. Brand’s total of 10 years and 6 months for four offences thus sits inside the most frequent band for the single offence of rape, while his nine-year rape term sits below the pooled average—the average pulled upward by the category 1 cases the judge declined to find here. Both instruments are printed because they answer different questions: the guideline answers what this case, as categorised, was worth; the distribution answers what the courts in fact hand down. Release is also statutory, not personal: offenders serving standard determinate sentences of four years or more for serious sexual or violent offences are released on licence at the two-thirds point—in the Sentencing Council’s own words, quoted by The Times on sentencing day—a rule made in 2020 for sentences of seven years or more and extended to four years or more in 2022. For Brand the arithmetic is seven years in custody, then licence, with the sex offenders’ register for life.

The third baseline is the funnel, because a historic prosecution is ordinary in kind and rare in outcome. England and Wales set no time limit for indictable offences; the six-month limit in section 127 of the Magistrates’ Courts Act 1980 reaches summary offences only. Prosecuting offences years after the event is standing practice, institutionalised since the inquiries of the 2010s: the CPS’s rape and serious sexual offences units handle non-recent cases as a category, and a conviction may rest on a complainant’s testimony alone if the jury is sure. The CPS is an independent body of career prosecutors, separate from the police; a charge must pass its Full Code Test—sufficient evidence for a realistic prospect of conviction, and the public interest. What the funnel does to cases is in the House of Lords Library’s figures: of 71,227 rapes recorded by police in 2024, 2,223 had resulted in a charge, 3.1 per cent, down from 7.5 per cent in 2016–17, while of cases that reach prosecution, about 53 per cent end in conviction. The figures are a snapshot of outcomes still maturing, filed at that grade; their shape is not in dispute. A case like this one—historic, testimonial, charged, tried, and split by the jury—is the far end of that funnel.

3. The Same Facts in an American Courtroom: Four Structural Differences

First, time. In England and Wales there is no limitations clock on these offences at all. In the United States of the 2000s, the clock was the case: state limitation periods for rape were finite and varied—six years in California for offences of that era, ten years in Texas for adult sexual assault, four years in Florida for adult sexual battery, on the state data compiled by RAINN—and the Supreme Court held in Stogner v. California, 539 U.S. 607 (2003), that a law reviving a prosecution after the period has expired violates the Ex Post Facto Clause. On the facts of the convicted counts, 2004 to 2009, a criminal prosecution in most American jurisdictions would have been time-barred long before 2023. The remedy American law built instead is civil: lookback windows that reopen expired civil claims for a fixed period. Brand’s own American file is exactly that instrument—the New York case filed in November 2023 under the Adult Survivors Act, which proceeds toward trial, as the desk’s November 9 report filed it.

Second, publication. In England and Wales, once proceedings are active—from arrest or charge—the strict liability rule of the Contempt of Court Act 1981 makes it a contempt, regardless of intent, to publish anything creating a substantial risk that the course of justice will be seriously impeded or prejudiced; the CPS’s prosecution guidance states the rule in those terms. Its operation is visible inside this very story: The Times held six further women’s accounts until the trial had ended, and said so. In the United States, the First Amendment runs the other way: in Nebraska Press Association v. Stuart, 427 U.S. 539 (1976), the Supreme Court struck down a gag order on pre-trial reporting, holding prior restraints on publication, in Chief Justice Burger’s words, “the most serious and the least tolerable infringement on First Amendment rights”; American practice manages prejudice through jury selection, venue, and instruction rather than through silence.

Third, the jury. England and Wales have permitted majority verdicts since the Criminal Justice Act 1967: after at least two hours’ deliberation a jury may convict by 11 to 1 or 10 to 2. American criminal convictions require unanimity, in federal court by long practice and in state courts since Ramos v. Louisiana, 590 U.S. 83 (2020). In this case the distinction is recorded and moot: the Metropolitan Police state that Brand’s verdicts, guilty and not guilty alike, were unanimous. The majority route was available to the jury and, on the record, was not used.

Fourth, the law of the sentence over time. An English court sentencing a historic offender applies the modern guideline, capped at the maximum penalty available on the date of the offence; where the offences predate the modern maxima, the cap bites, as it did for Rolf Harris, whose offences of 1968 to 1986 were sentenced in 2014 under the ceilings of their own era. Brand’s convicted conduct, 2004 to 2009, postdates the Sexual Offences Act 2003, in force from May 1, 2004, so the modern ceiling applied to him directly and the cap had nothing to cut. American law binds the sentence to the offence date from the other side: the same ex post facto principle that decided Stogner forbids applying a harsher later sentencing law to earlier conduct. The two systems thus meet historic crime with opposite instruments—London with today’s guideline under yesterday’s ceiling, Washington with yesterday’s law entire—and the difference is structural, not a commentary on this defendant.

4. The Targeting Question: Both Camps’ Exhibits, and the Precedent Line

The defenders’ exhibits are four, and each is a dated thing. The first is timing: Brand’s turn against the political parties, the pharmaceutical companies, and the media he used to work for began a decade before the allegations aired—his Trews programme launched in 2014—and the prosecution followed the turn, not the offences. The second is sequence: no charge in this case predates publication; the case began as a newspaper and television investigation in September 2023, and the sentencing judge himself wrote the sequence into the record—“Your status protected you until 2023 when journalists collected and published the allegations against you.” The third is tolerance: the broadcasters’ own post-2023 inquiries record that complaints from Brand’s BBC and Channel 4 years were not acted on at the time—the BBC’s review of his 2006–2008 radio tenure and Channel 4’s uninvestigated 2009 complaint are filed in the desk’s November 9 report—from which the defenders argue that the industry protected him while he was useful and withdrew the protection when he was not. The fourth is the platform correspondence of September 2023: on September 19 and 20, Dame Caroline Dinenage, chair of the Commons Culture, Media and Sport Committee, wrote to TikTok, X, Rumble, and Meta asking whether they would join YouTube in suspending Brand’s ability to earn money, before any charge existed; Rumble refused in public, calling the request deeply inappropriate and dangerous. An open letter to Brand’s lawyers, published Monday over the name of R. Leland Lehrman, builds these exhibits into the camp’s fullest statement, styling Brand a political prisoner; the supporter petition shared on November 12 makes the same argument in five demands.

Two dated facts sit inside the defenders’ sequence, and the record carries both. YouTube suspended Brand’s advertising income on September 19, 2023, under its creator responsibility policy—before the committee’s letters of September 19 and 20, not after them; the first platform act preceded the parliamentary ask. And the journalists’ own account of their investigation, attributed to them as their account, runs the file back further than the broadcast: Rosamund Urwin of The Sunday Times has said she began speaking to sources in January 2019; she and Charlotte Wace describe an investigation of nearly four years, contacting more than 500 sources, with the women coming forward in the period after the #MeToo movement; Channel 4’s own review dates the Dispatches commission to December 2019, the collaboration formalised in autumn 2022. On the journalists’ account, the file opened in 2019, before the pandemic-era turn the timing exhibit treats as the cause. The desk does not reconcile the two timelines; it prints them, dated, side by side.

The counter-camp’s exhibit is the precedent line: the same machinery, in the same era, against men who never left the establishment. Rolf Harris, a fixture of British broadcasting for half a century, was convicted in 2014 under Operation Yewtree on 12 counts of indecent assault for offences from 1968 to 1986 and sentenced to 5 years and 9 months; one conviction was later overturned on appeal and the sentence stood. Kevin Spacey, tried at Southwark Crown Court in 2023 on allegations from 2001 to 2013 brought by four men, was acquitted by the jury on all nine counts—the same court, the same offence class, the opposite outcome. Huw Edwards, for years the BBC’s principal news presenter, pleaded guilty in 2024 to three counts of making indecent images of children and received six months, suspended for two years. Harvey Weinstein, the defining insider of his industry, was convicted in New York in 2020 and sentenced to 23 years; the conviction was overturned in 2024 for improperly admitted testimony; at retrial in 2025 he was convicted on one count, acquitted on one, and a third count was dropped after two juries hung; he stands separately convicted in Los Angeles in 2022, with 16 years. The line is printed as the counter-camp files it: the system prosecuted insiders, acquitted one of them outright, and overturned its own largest conviction on a point of law.

The case’s own internal checks are the analysts’ answer, and they are also record, not argument. The same jury that convicted Brand on four counts acquitted him on three, unanimously. The judge refused the prosecution’s higher category, refused fame as an aggravator, refused a dangerousness finding, excluded the documentary’s allegations and the acquitted counts from the sentence entirely, and bounded the mitigation to a single year. The charging decision was taken by the CPS, applying a published two-stage test, after a police investigation in which Brand was interviewed under caution four times. The defence’s contamination argument was put to the jury in closing, and the application to stay the case over the publicity had been refused as unpersuasive before the trial began. Legal commentators’ answer to the lawfare claim, as filed in the week’s explainers, is that no procedural irregularity has been identified in the record; a sentence appeal is, in the assessment of Raj Chada of Hodge Jones & Allen, a solicitor not involved in the case, the most likely application. The paper weighs neither camp. It prints the exhibits, the dates that check them, and the precedent line, and leaves the cocked hat where the record leaves it.

5. The Martyr Argument: Three Positions, All Attributed

The first position is his alternative-media base’s, and it is secular. In this reading the imprisonment is a coordinated takedown: allegations from 2004 to 2009, held for two decades, deployed when the man holding 10 million followers on X became a threat to the governments and companies he attacks. Megyn Kelly, broadcasting within minutes of the verdicts, called the case a political witch hunt, as reported; Elon Musk, before the sentence, called the expected punishment “unjust,” as the desk’s November 9 report filed. The petition and the open letter belong to this position: Brand as a martyr for free speech and truth-telling, punished for the audience, not the acts. It is a position about the state, and it requires no theology.

The second position is his Christian following’s, and it is biblical. Its timeline is central to its account: the allegations aired in September 2023; Brand was baptised by immersion in the River Thames on April 28, 2024, with Bear Grylls beside him, describing the baptism as an opportunity to “leave the past behind,” an act of “surrender, undertaken in gratitude and in sincerity”; the charges came a year later, in April 2025. In this reading, faith found as the state closed in is the story, and the imprisonment is its trial. Outside Southwark Crown Court on sentencing day, supporters held a banner bearing crosses, in the Associated Press’s account as carried by BuzzFeed: “Russell Brand we stand with you. Christ was crucified for telling the truth. Russell is the truth.” Brand himself, in the dock, clenched a crucifix, the same account records. His prison message is this position’s text: innocence stated inside the faith, “something strange is happening,” and forgiveness extended downward to the men imprisoned with him, “people that Christ died to save, like you and me.”

The third position comes from inside the church the claim addresses, and it rejects the frame on theological grounds. Premier Christianity, on November 6, published the therapist Holly-Anna Petersen under the headline “Russell Brand’s rape conviction shows that forgiveness does not cancel justice”: God’s redemption, she argues, must never come at the expense of victims, and repentance is more than a public declaration—it is an honest recognition of the harm caused and a willingness to take responsibility. The Guardian’s examination of the conversion, published in the verdict’s aftermath and summarised in the Religion Media Centre’s bulletin of November 9, posed the question whether Brand “wore his new found faith as a cloak in an effort to deflect and distract from the seriousness of the allegations against him,” or whether the conversion is “a profound and sincere one”; it recorded Nick Spencer of the think tank Theos on the tension—“you want to affirm a sense of grace, a sense of forgiveness, of repentance and a new life, without ignoring the claims of justice”—and an Oxford academic’s description of the conversion’s manner as “very performative.” The Archbishop of York, Stephen Cottrell, who appeared on Brand’s podcast in 2019, responded through his office: abuse must never be excused, enabled, or tolerated, and acknowledging wrongdoing and remorse are vital to Christian life. From the supporting side inside the same church, Grylls posted on the morning of sentencing: “Brand’s faith seemed genuine to me at the time when I was a guest at his private baptism. It is the sick that need healing. Judgement is for the courts and God.” The paper adjudicates no one’s faith. It files the three positions as they stand: the martyr of the platforms, the convert in the river, and the church answering both with a doctrine of penance that runs through the sentence, not around it.

6. The Open Record at November 16, and the Week’s Disagreements

The appeal record is a pair of dates and an absence. No filing was confirmed in any reporting the desk found as of Monday. TMZ reported on November 9 that Brand’s lawyers were drawing up appeal papers; that is a report of preparation, tabloid grade, not a filing. The clocks are 28 days: notice of appeal against conviction is due by December 3, 2026, and against sentence by December 7, 2026, on the legal explainers’ account, which a defender’s published letter states in the same dates. The same 28 days is the window in which the Attorney General may be asked to refer the sentence as unduly lenient; no referral has been announced. What remains open otherwise stands as the November 9 report left it, with two movements: the police triage of the reports received during and after the trial—Detective Superintendent Andy Furphy said on BBC Breakfast on November 10 that officers were “in the process of triaging” them—and the Netflix documentary of November 13, which carries three of the six new accounts to a second platform. The New York civil case proceeds toward trial, unchanged in the week’s record; the lesser London civil claim stands at the grade the November 9 report gave it.

The disagreements the week carries are printed unresolved, in the house manner. First, the trial’s length: four weeks in the releases of the CPS and the Metropolitan Police, three weeks in The Times and several outlets; the conflict stands from the November 9 file and is not averaged here. Second, a deadline in the wild: one American aggregator printed the sentence-appeal deadline as “December 7, 2027”; the year is that source’s error, and the date is December 7, 2026. Third, the prosecutor’s name: the sentencing remarks and the CPS record Riel Karmy-Jones KC; one secondary explainer rendered the first name “Eloise,” and the desk follows the record. Fourth, the Littlehey transfer: reported November 13 by tabloid and aggregator sources without official confirmation, and since confirmed by the only witness whose account is first-hand, Brand himself, in the message that opened this report. The final paragraph is the first paragraph’s restatement, as the form requires: one week after a jury’s unanimous verdicts and a judge’s reasoned sentence of 10 years and 6 months, the case has produced a disciplinary investigation into a message from a cell, a set of baselines by which the sentence can be measured in its own system’s numbers, an American comparison that shows how much of the outcome is the system and not the man, two camps’ exhibits on why he was prosecuted at all, and a martyr argument conducted in three attributed voices. The desk files all of it, attributed and graded, and weighs none of it.

 The Filed Clippings

 Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective, a source with a position, printed because it is useful, and described by what it says. The desk’s report is the only part of this file stamped objective. Twelve items.

 

 SubjectiveBBC—reporting of the prison-message investigation and the government reaction (November 16, 2026)The day’s lead, from the broadcaster: Downing Street’s confirmation that the message is being urgently investigated, the spokesman’s statement of the rules in full, the Foreign Secretary’s words to Sky News, and the London Victims’ Commissioner’s assessment on the Today programme.

 SubjectivePress Association wire—the investigation, the deeming understanding, and the Bronson precedent (November 16, 2026), as syndicated across the regional pressThe wire account carrying the operative sentence of the day—that a prisoner is deemed to have broken the rules by giving comments to a family member knowing they will be published—and the 2022 precedent of a 28-day telephone restriction imposed on another prisoner for a message sent to a broadcaster.

 SubjectiveThe Sun and the broadcast transcripts—the message’s text, the view count, and the Littlehey transfer (November 13–16, 2026)The fullest renderings of the message as read aloud, the tabloid’s count of more than 150,000 views by Monday, its claim about the prisoner’s earnings from premium followers on Rumble, and the first reporting of the transfer from Wandsworth, since confirmed by the message itself.

 SubjectiveThe Prison Rules 1999 and the Prison Act 1952—rules 8, 34, 53A, 55, and 55A, with R (Nilsen) v Governor of HMP Full Sutton (Court of Appeal, 2004)The framework documents: communication by leave or privilege, the standing-order bar on correspondence material intended for publication about the prisoner’s crime, the governor’s and the independent adjudicator’s punishments, and the appellate judgment upholding the publication bar against a prisoner who wished to publish his account.

 SubjectiveSentencing Academy—Snapshot of rape sentencing (September 2026), on Ministry of Justice Criminal Justice Statistics to December 2025The distribution the report measures against: 1,602 rape convictions in 2025, the modal band of 10 to 15 years at 26 per cent, about a fifth of sentences above 15 years, and the average custodial term’s rise from about 8 years in 2010 to almost 11.

 SubjectiveSentencing Council—the rape guideline, and The Times’ sentencing report (November 9, 2026)The grid and its application: the 4-to-19-year offence range, the category starting points from which category 2B’s 8 years is taken, the sexual assault range, and the Council’s own statement, carried in the sentencing report, that the two-thirds release point is a general rule for sentences of four years or more for serious sexual and violent offences.

 SubjectiveCrown Prosecution Service—prosecution guidance on contempt of court and the Contempt of Court Act 1981The strict liability rule as the prosecuting authority states it: proceedings active from arrest, publication creating a substantial risk of serious prejudice punishable as contempt regardless of intent—the rule under which the six further accounts were held until the verdicts.

 SubjectiveFirst Amendment Encyclopedia (Middle Tennessee State University)—Nebraska Press Association v. Stuart, 427 U.S. 539 (1976); with Stogner v. California, 539 U.S. 607 (2003), and Ramos v. Louisiana, 590 U.S. 83 (2020)The American side of the structural comparison: the unanimous 1976 judgment striking down a pre-trial gag order as a prior restraint, the 2003 holding that an expired limitations period cannot be revived, and the 2020 holding that state criminal convictions require a unanimous jury.

 SubjectiveThe Times and The Sunday Times—the six further women (November 12–13, 2026), and the Netflix documentary Russell Brand: Open Secret (November 13, 2026)The accounts withheld until the trial ended, incidents alleged from 2005 to 2015, the papers’ statement that extensive corroboration steps were taken and no sources were paid, the absence of a response from Brand’s side, and the film that carries three of the accounts. Journalism, filed as journalism; none of it has been tested in a court.

 SubjectiveTaylor Tailored Legal Services and the week’s legal explainers—the appeal clocks and the likely grounds (November 2026)The procedural map of what happens next: 28 days from verdict for conviction and from sentence for sentence, the single-judge filter, the unduly-lenient referral window, and the assessment, echoed by a solicitor uninvolved in the case, that a sentence appeal is the probable route.

 SubjectivePremier Christianity—“Russell Brand’s rape conviction shows that forgiveness does not cancel justice” (November 6, 2026); The Guardian’s conversion examination, as summarised by the Religion Media Centre (November 9, 2026)The church’s internal argument in its two fullest statements: the case for penance as recognition, responsibility, and consequence, set against the celebration of a public conversion; and the cloak-or-crutch question, with the theologians and the Archbishop of York’s office on the record, and the baptism’s defender beside them.

 SubjectiveR. Leland Lehrman—“Russell Brand, Political Prisoner,” an open letter to Brand’s lawyers (November 16, 2026), with the “Free Russell Brand” petitionThe defenders’ fullest published statement: the platform letters of September 2023 set out with their dates and addressees, the Assange parallel, the five demands, and the appeal deadlines stated as the camp states them. A partisan source, filed as one; its dated exhibits are the parts the report above checks against the record.

### Air Travel Returns Largely to Normal at 300 Cancelled by 0900 Against 55 Down at Dawn, the Secretary Puts the Weekend&rsquo;s Cost in Billions and Asks Congress for $50 Billion, Beijing Confirms Shenzhen in Words That Name Neither Nuclear Arms Nor Iran, and the Petition for Mr. Huang Passes 168,000 While Alaska&rsquo;s Count Still Waits

Filed as: Edition No. 55 — The Midday Watch · 2026-11-16T12:00:00-05:00 · https://objectivedailynews.com/editions/2026-11-16-midday-watch.html

The Midday File — The Desk’s Report

 Objective

 Air Travel Returns Largely to Normal at 300 Cancelled by 0900 Against 55 Down at Dawn, the Secretary Puts the Weekend’s Cost in Billions and Asks Congress for $50 Billion, Beijing Confirms Shenzhen in Words That Name Neither Nuclear Arms Nor Iran, and the Petition for Mr. Huang Passes 168,000 While Alaska’s Count Still Waits

 The midday file: a recovery morning counted at 300 cancelled by 0900 against 55 down at dawn and thousands on each of the three days before it, and a funding fight opened in the same hours; a host’s confirmation in Beijing that names world peace and strategic stability and names neither of Washington’s subjects; a denial on the radar that answers for the drones and not for the machine; a count that spent another morning where Saturday left it; a petition past 168,000 with the board still silent; and an Asian close in the red, read at noon in New York as the chairman begins to speak.

 By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 1200 ET, Monday, November 16, 2026. This edition continues the file from Edition No. 54, the Overnight Watch, collected at 0400 today, from Edition No. 53, the Midnight Watch, collected at 0000 today, from Edition No. 52, the Evening Watch, collected at 1800 on Sunday, and from Edition No. 50, the Midday Watch, collected at 1200 on Sunday. Those editions stand unrevised, as a log stands. Where the midday figures differ from the figures those editions carried, the difference is stated here, in the open.

The Midday in Brief: A Recovery Counted in the Hundreds, a Confirmation in Beijing, and a Count That Did Not Move

The midday’s corrections run toward normal on the ground and toward precision in the statements, and the count in Alaska did not move at all. United States air travel largely returned to normal on Monday after more than 18,000 flight cancellations over three days, in the wire account filed below: as of 0900 Eastern there were just 300 flight cancellations and 1,500 delays, down from more than 2,300 cancelled and 11,000 delayed on Sunday, against 55 of Monday’s flights cancelled as of Sunday evening in the overnight file. A second account counted 533 cancelled by 0700, in the morning account filed below, and the desk prints the two Monday readings apart, at their hours, in the Cocked Hat. In Beijing, the Foreign Ministry’s spokeswoman confirmed the Shenzhen meeting in words set out below and, asked about nuclear arms control and Iran, named neither, in the confirmation account filed below. In Alaska, the Press’s count at 0840 on Monday stands exactly where Saturday left it—Ms. Peltola 140,637, Senator Sullivan 129,424, an estimated 97 percent counted—and the race stands uncalled, in the markets account filed below. The petition for Mr. Huang passed 168,000 signatures on Monday, in the comeback account filed below, and the board’s answer is still not in the file. At noon, as this edition collects, the central bank chairman opens the conference on artificial intelligence and productivity in San Francisco. The desk takes the files in that order.

What the morning settled is the shape of the recovery and the words of the confirmation. What it left open is the root cause of Friday’s stop, the condition of the radar at Al-Riffa, the call in Alaska, and the board’s first word.

The Airlines at Midday: 300 Cancelled by 0900 in the Wire’s Count, 533 by 0700 in the Morning Account, and a Funding Fight Opened on CNBC

Monday’s recovery is real in every account, and its exact size depends on the account, and the desk prints the readings at their hours. The wire account above counts 300 cancellations and 1,500 delays as of 0900, down from more than 2,300 cancelled and 11,000 delayed on Sunday, and puts the three days together at more than 18,000 cancellations stemming from Friday’s ground stop, the longest for 25 years, suspected to have been caused by a single router installed during routine maintenance. The morning account above counts about 8,365 flights delayed and 533 cancelled nationwide by 0700, against 26,392 delayed and 2,858 cancelled on Sunday in the same account’s figures, with American holding the largest number of Monday cancellations at 157, followed by SkyWest at 38, and Dallas-Fort Worth and Chicago O’Hare the origin airports with the highest numbers. A third account counted about 250 flights cancelled by 0400, in the operations account filed below, which records that American expected a largely normal Monday and did not anticipate additional widespread cancellations tied to the stop, and that Delta warned some delays and cancellations could continue. The overnight file’s opening figure, 55 of Monday’s flights cancelled as of Sunday evening, stands at the head of the series; Tuesday’s cancellations stand at 68 due to be cancelled, in the morning account, ahead of the Thanksgiving travel period. No second stop was ordered on Monday in any account the desk read.

The official statements at midday are about money, and they divide in the open. Speaking on CNBC on Monday, Secretary Duffy estimated the economic impact of the disruptions, which also delayed nearly 28,000 flights, in “billions of dollars,” and said the system is telegraphing to the American people that it needs investment and that now is the time to do a big dollar amount to modernize it, in the wire account above; his request stands at $50 billion, raised on Friday from $30 billion, for air traffic control and airports, in the same account, which notes the Administration is still using aging equipment including Compaq computers, floppy disks and paper strips. Democrats in Congress answered that the Secretary has spent only $1 billion of the initial $12.5 billion approved last year, and that they want hearings into what led to the communications disruptions, in the same account; the Secretary and Republicans want quick action in the final weeks before the current Congress goes home and the Democrats take over in January, in the same account. The airlines’ own figure stands apart from the Secretary’s: the four largest carriers face an estimated $345 million earnings hit, in a brokerage estimate carried in the estimate account filed below, which puts the combined pretax figure at about $345 million with a range of roughly $270 million to $430 million. On cause, the Administration’s Sunday explanation stands unamended at midday: excessive data overwhelmed parts of the telecommunications network, two potential sources were identified at Amarillo, Texas, and El Dorado, Arkansas, the network provider blocked those locations, and the underlying cause is still under investigation, in the operations account; the Secretary said on Sunday that the Administration still does not know what ultimately caused a problem in maintenance work done thousands of times before without issue, in the morning account. Settled: the recovery, and the size of the ask. Open: the root cause, and whether Congress pays.

Shenzhen at Midday: The Host’s Words Are World Peace and Strategic Stability, and Neither of Washington’s Subjects Is Named

Beijing’s confirmation, the overnight file’s largest fact, gained its text at midday, and the text is printed here at its exact width. “They will exchange views in depth on safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability in major-power relations, which is of groundbreaking significance,” spokeswoman Mao Ning told the ministry’s daily briefing on Monday, in the confirmation account above; she said it would be the first face-to-face meeting of the three countries’ heads of state, and that all three are founding members of the United Nations and permanent members of its Security Council. A reporter then put Washington’s agenda to her—nuclear arms control and Iran—and Mao named neither, saying in Chinese that the three leaders would exchange views in depth on major issues bearing on global peace and that China would release information on the meeting in a timely manner, in the same account. The ministry’s confirmation came after the same holding answer at five briefings between November 4 and 13, in the same account. The host’s own announcement stands in the host account filed below: President Xi will host Presidents Trump and Putin on Thursday, November 19, on the sidelines of the APEC leaders’ meeting of November 18 and 19, which Xi chairs; the statement gave the date and the venue and no details of the agenda.

The other capitals’ words stand where the week left them, and two more voices joined the file on Monday. The Gulf at Midday: A Denial That Answers for the Drones, an Ambassador’s Sentence, and No Assessment of the Radar

The Central Command spokesman’s sentence from Sunday night stands in the midnight file at its own width: no impacts to American forces, and nothing said about the radar itself. Europe at Midday: Moscow Hopes to Hear Directly From the Europeans, Brussels Promises Maximum Support and Maximum Pressure, and a Prisoner Exchange Is Prepared

Europe’s file gained a Monday statement from Moscow, and it is a statement about Europe’s statements. The Kremlin’s spokesman said on Monday that the Union’s latest statements on the Ukraine negotiations suggest a reluctance to contribute to the peace process, and that Moscow continues to hope to hear directly from the Europeans how its position can help in those efforts, in the Moscow account filed below. The spokesman recalled that the Commission’s president and her colleagues in Brussels have stated that unconditional support for Ukraine will be maintained and that the bloc will maintain the line of increasing pressure on Russia to force it to participate in the peace process, in the same account; he insisted that the negotiations have so far been coordinated in a trilateral format among Moscow, Washington and Kyiv, and that Russia does not want a temporary truce but a peace that will last for many years, in the same account. Against that stands the Commission president’s Sunday sentence, in the same account: Europe will participate actively in the peace talks through the E5 + EU format, guaranteeing in the meantime maximum support for Kyiv and maximum pressure on Moscow. No contact from Europe’s negotiators to Moscow stands in the midday file; the spokesman’s Sunday answer, that they have not yet attempted to make contact, stands unamended, and the team’s composition stands in the team account filed below: Germany, France, the United Kingdom, Italy and Poland, with the Commission and the Council, fielding national security advisers in the account’s expectation, with no negotiators yet named.

One channel in the file did move on Monday, and it is the prisoners’ channel. Russia’s human-rights commissioner said on Monday that contacts are being maintained with her Ukrainian counterpart with a view to a major exchange of prisoners of war and to organizing a humanitarian mission in Kostiantynivka, in the Moscow account above: “We are in regular contact, and we are preparing a major exchange, which has been announced.” No number and no date for the exchange stand in the account. The American envoys’ weekend sentence stands in the same file: Washington is working to incorporate the European partners directly into the next round of the trilateral talks, with the Foreign Ministry in Moscow questioning whether the Kremlin has given its approval for that participation, in the same account. The next fact in the Europe file remains a telephone call that has not been made, and the first fact in the prisoners’ file is now a preparation that has been stated.

France and Spain at Midday: A Strike Tomorrow and a Bill on Thursday in Paris, and Three Monday Polls in Madrid That Agree on the Majority and Differ on the Socialists

France’s file at midday is a calendar, unchanged since the weekend, with its two dates now one and three days off. The unions’ nationwide strike stands on Tuesday, November 17, the eighth anniversary of the Yellow Vest movement, called after the rejection of the government’s 0.6 percent minimum-wage promise; the police bill—a presumption of legitimate self-defence for an officer who fires, a licence to kill in its critics’ phrase in the accounts—goes to the Senate on Thursday, November 19, in the Senate account filed below. Saturday’s fifth day of protest stands closed at 106,000 nationwide in the Interior Ministry’s count and about 200,000 in the organisers’, with about 400 people stopped nationwide and 108 held in custody in Paris in the fullest account filed overnight. A sixth Saturday is called for November 21. No new statement from the government or the unions stands in the midday file.

Spain’s campaign gained three Monday polls, and they agree on the outcome and differ on the Socialists by four points. The three surveys, the first since the campaign’s launch, are set out in the polls account filed below. The daily tracking puts the Popular Party at 31.5 percent, the Socialists at 30.3—past 30 percent for the first time in that series and their best figure since the 2023 election—and Vox at 18.0, with the two right parties’ combined seats above 190 against 176 needed. A second poll projects 201 to 205 seats for the Popular Party and Vox combined, with the Socialists at 26.1 percent and 102 to 104 seats. The third, in the survey account filed below, puts the Popular Party at 31.5 percent and 128 seats, the Socialists at 26.9 and 109, and Vox at 19.0 and 66, down four seats, with the right bloc at 194 seats in all. In all three, the Socialists gained ground on the reading before, and in all three the right’s majority stands. The state survey’s Socialist lead stands against all three where the week left it. The head-to-head debate between Mr. S&aacute;nchez and Mr. Feij&oacute;o stands on Thursday, November 19; polls may publish until November 23; Spain votes on November 29.

 The Clippings Filed With This Edition

 Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective—a source with a position, printed because it is useful—and described by what it says. The desk’s report is the only item in this edition stamped objective. 33 items.

 

 SubjectiveReuters — air travel largely returns to normal on Monday, 300 cancelled by 0900, and the Secretary on CNBC puts the impact in billionsUnited States air travel largely returned to normal on Monday after more than 18,000 flight cancellations over three days stemming from Friday’s longest ground stop for 25 years, suspected to have been caused by a single router installed during routine maintenance. Speaking on CNBC, Transportation Secretary Duffy estimated the economic impact of the disruptions, which also delayed nearly 28,000 flights, would be in “billions of dollars.” On Monday, as of 9 a.m. Eastern, there were just 300 flight cancellations and 1,500 delays, down from more than 2,300 canceled and 11,000 delayed on Sunday, according to FlightAware. The four largest airlines face an estimated $345 million earnings hit, according to a brokerage. The Secretary on Friday raised his request for funding for air traffic control and airports to $50 billion from $30 billion; the Administration is still using aging equipment including Compaq computers, floppy disks and paper strips. Democrats in Congress say the Secretary has spent only $1 billion of the initial $12.5 billion approved last year, and want hearings into what led to the disruptions. The Secretary said the system is telegraphing to the American people that it needs investment, and that now is the time to do a big dollar amount to modernize it.

 SubjectiveNBC News — travel largely returning to normal on Monday, 533 cancelled by 0700, and 68 of Tuesday’s due to be cancelledAir travel across the United States was largely returning to normal on Monday, although some disruption persisted as airlines scrambled to get back on schedule after the nationwide ground stop. By 7 a.m. Eastern on Monday about 8,365 flights were delayed and 533 cancelled nationwide, a dramatic drop from the 26,392 delayed and 2,858 cancelled flights on Sunday, according to FlightAware. American Airlines had the largest number of canceled flights on Monday at 157, followed by SkyWest with 38; Dallas-Fort Worth and Chicago O’Hare were the origin airports with the highest numbers of cancellations. Just 68 flights were due to be cancelled on Tuesday, as passengers gear up for Thanksgiving travel. The Administration lifted the ground stop at 8:15 p.m. on Friday; it was the longest nationwide halt since September 11, 2001, and the Homeland Security Secretary said authorities had found no evidence of a cyberattack. The contractor had been working on replacing a copper line with a fiber line at a remote site in El Dorado, Arkansas; the Secretary said on Sunday that the replacement triggered problems with another recently replaced router in Amarillo, Texas, which started broadcasting and overloading routers at other centers. The Administration said it still does not know what ultimately caused the problem in maintenance work done thousands of times before without issue.

 SubjectiveConsumerAffairs — operations approaching normal on Monday morning, about 250 cancelled by 0400, and the Administration’s Sunday explanationUnited States airline operations were moving toward normal on Monday morning, November 16, following a weekend spent recovering from Friday’s nationwide ground stop, although some travelers continued to face canceled flights. About 250 flights were canceled by 4 a.m. Eastern on Monday, according to FlightAware; that follows a Sunday when the tracker recorded 2,291 cancellations as of 3 p.m. American said it did not anticipate additional widespread cancellations tied to the ground stop, and Delta reported progress, saying on Sunday that most flights were operating normally. Friday’s disruption began after a technical problem developed around 3:30 p.m. Eastern; the system stabilized and traffic resumed at 8:15 p.m., nearly five hours later. In an explanation released on Sunday, the Administration said excessive data overwhelmed parts of its telecommunications network, disrupting aircraft communications and radar feeds; investigators identified two potential sources, a radar facility in Amarillo, Texas, and a radio communications site in El Dorado, Arkansas, and the network provider blocked those locations, helping stabilize the network, while the underlying cause continued to be investigated.

 SubjectiveReuters — the four largest airlines face a $345 million hit, in a brokerage estimateThe four largest United States airlines face an estimated $345 million earnings hit after the nationwide ground stop on Friday disrupted flights through the weekend, according to a brokerage estimate published on Monday. The estimate puts the cost to American, Delta, United and Southwest at about $345 million pretax combined, with a range of roughly $270 million to $430 million. The Transportation Secretary said on a Sunday programme that operations would probably be fully normal by Monday, as airlines worked to reposition aircraft and crews and restore schedules; earlier on Monday, on CNBC, he urged Congress to swiftly fund air traffic control upgrades after saying the disruption likely caused billions in losses.

 SubjectiveAsiaToday — China confirms the first Xi-Trump-Putin summit for Thursday at APEC in ShenzhenChina confirmed on Monday that President Xi Jinping will host United States President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin for the first trilateral summit of the three leaders on Thursday, November 19, on the sidelines of this week’s APEC leaders’ meeting in Shenzhen. The 33rd APEC Economic Leaders’ Meeting runs on November 18 and 19, with Xi chairing the gathering of leaders from the forum’s 21 member economies. China’s Foreign Ministry announced the meeting in a brief statement on Monday, giving the date and the venue but no details of the agenda. The White House and the Kremlin had already confirmed the plan, and Beijing’s statement was the first official confirmation from the Chinese side. The three presidents have never met together in a trilateral format before. Discussions are expected to cover global conflicts, artificial intelligence and the reduction of nuclear weapons, according to reporting on the meeting.

 SubjectiveSilent Dossier — China confirms Xi will host Trump and Putin in Shenzhen, and will not name nuclear arms or Iran as topicsChina’s foreign ministry confirmed on Monday, November 16, that Xi Jinping will meet Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump in Shenzhen on Thursday, November 19; it was the host’s first confirmation, three days after the White House announced the meeting and two days after the Kremlin did. “They will exchange views in depth on safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability in major-power relations, which is of groundbreaking significance,” spokeswoman Mao Ning told the ministry’s daily briefing; she said it would be the first face-to-face meeting of the three countries’ heads of state. A Japanese reporter then put Washington’s agenda to her, nuclear arms control and Iran; Mao named neither, saying the leaders would exchange views in depth on major issues bearing on global peace and that China would release information in a timely manner. The ministry had given the same holding answer at five briefings between November 4 and 13. The United Nations Secretary-General said in Manila on Monday that the United Nations is ready to support a denuclearisation programme and to be fully engaged in it, adding that it is not yet guaranteed the parties will get there, and called on Iran for a serious diplomatic process to end a state of neither peace nor war. The account also carries the German Chancellor’s words from the Dublin meeting of November 13, “Please, no surprises,” addressed to Washington.

 SubjectiveCandid Dragon — the Monday morning briefing: the President leaves for Asia, a third carrier reaches the Middle East, and Congress gets its first briefing on the stopThe morning briefing for Monday, November 16, checked against at least two outlets or an official source on each item.  SubjectiveThe carrier account — a third carrier enters the region, new strikes ‘highly unlikely,’ Tehran still at war, and a drone at Khor MorThe USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group entered the Central Command area of operations on Sunday, joining the USS George H.W. Bush and the USS George Washington, both already operating in the Arabian Sea, in a force of more than 20 Navy ships enforcing a blockade of Iranian ports; an American official said the three-carrier presence is expected to be temporary as strike groups rotate, though all three could stay if necessary. The Guards said they launched six drones at an American air defence radar system at the Al-Riffa helicopter base in Bahrain on Sunday, describing the strike as a response to American aggression and claiming a successful impact; Bahrain’s military said it intercepted the attacks before they hit their targets. The President told reporters on Sunday that new strikes on Iran are highly unlikely as long as negotiations keep making progress, and that the United States could hit Iran’s nuclear facilities within five minutes if needed. Iran’s deputy foreign minister said in a televised interview that Tehran is preparing for three scenarios—diplomacy, economic blockade and military aggression—and that from a legal perspective Iran is still in a state of war; he listed Iran’s demands as a permanent end to the war on all fronts, removal of the blockade, resolution of the frozen-assets issue, and lifting of certain sanctions including those on oil. Parliament Speaker Ghalibaf said the conflict could end if Washington accepted Iran’s logical conditions and warned that if the United States resumes strikes, Iran’s forces would determine the geography of battle. Separately, a drone struck the Khor Mor gas field in Iraq’s Sulaymaniyah province on Sunday, setting off a large fire and cutting nearly 2,800 megawatts of regional power generation; no group has claimed it, Kurdish officials called it a terrorist attack, and the Iraqi prime minister’s office ordered a joint investigation with the Kurdish authorities. The account also carries the whistleblower complaint filed on Friday by an Army major who survived the March 1 drone attack on the Port Shuaiba command post in Kuwait, and the President’s scheduled Monday meeting in Washington with Qatar’s prime minister.

 SubjectiveAl Jazeera — Iran says it targets a United States radar in Bahrain: what is known, in orderThe Guards say they launched six drones at a United States air defence radar system at Bahrain’s Riffa Air Base in response to what they describe as hostile American actions. The Guards said they struck the radar, according to a statement carried by the Fars agency; the Interior Ministry issued two alerts within about three hours, the first at about 4:30 a.m. local time, and the Defence Force said its air defence systems thwarted several Iranian aerial attacks targeting the kingdom. On Friday the Guards said they destroyed a United States early-warning radar system in Bahrain in retaliation for what they described as an air attack on a telecommunications tower in southern Iran; Central Command denied the claim, saying it had shot down two drones and there were no injuries or damage. The American military said it intercepted two Iranian drones on Friday but had yet to comment on Sunday’s claim in the account’s file.

 SubjectiveMilitary.com — Iran targets a military base in a second Bahrain drone attack in three days, and the Embassy warns AmericansIran launched a drone attack against a military base in Bahrain, its second strike on the country in the past three days. The Guards said they used six drones to target the United States air defense radar facility at the al-Riffa air base on Sunday, days after similarly firing drones at Bahrain on Friday. Bahrain’s military said its air defense systems intercepted and destroyed the drones. The base hosts critical American air defense infrastructure, including a key early-warning radar site, and supports American rotary-wing operations. The American Embassy in Bahrain on Sunday warned Americans to exercise heightened vigilance, adding that there could be possible flight cancellations, airspace closures and other travel disruptions after the drone attacks. The American military said it intercepted two Iranian attack drones headed toward Bahrain on Sunday, while the Guards claimed they struck an early warning radar system in the kingdom; the United States denied Iran’s claim. The strikes break a two-month lull in Iranian attacks on Gulf states, testing negotiations aimed at ending the eight-month conflict and reopening the Strait of Hormuz.

 SubjectiveDem&oacute;crata — Russia sees in the Union’s messages a lack of willingness to promote peace, and the commissioners prepare a major exchangeRussian authorities indicated on Monday that the latest European Union statements about negotiations concerning Ukraine suggest a reluctance to contribute to the peace process, although they underlined that Moscow continues to hope to hear directly from the Europeans how its position can help in those diplomatic efforts. The Kremlin’s spokesman recalled that the Commission’s president and her colleagues in Brussels have stated that unconditional support for Ukraine will be maintained and that the bloc will maintain the line of increasing pressure on Russia in order to force it to participate in the peace process. The spokesman also pointed out that so far the negotiations have been coordinated in a trilateral format, referring to contacts between Moscow, Washington and Kyiv, and insisted that Russia does not want a temporary truce, but rather a peace that will last for many years and centuries. The statements come after the Commission’s president reiterated on Sunday that Europe will participate actively in the peace talks through the E5 + EU format—the institutions alongside Germany, France, the United Kingdom, Italy and Poland—while guaranteeing maximum support for Kyiv and maximum pressure on Moscow. The heads of state and government of the Twenty-Seven agreed on Friday at the Dublin summit to set the European negotiating team in motion. The American envoys said after their recent meetings in Moscow and Dublin that Washington is working to incorporate the European partners directly into the next round of trilateral talks, although the Russian Foreign Ministry has questioned whether the Kremlin has given its approval for that participation. Meanwhile, the Russian human-rights commissioner confirmed on Monday that contacts are being maintained with her Ukrainian counterpart with a view to a major exchange of prisoners of war and to organizing a humanitarian mission in Kostiantynivka: “We are in regular contact and we are preparing a major exchange, which has been announced.”

 SubjectiveEuropean Global Times — Europe picks a five-nation team for the Ukraine talks, and no negotiators have been namedEuropean leaders have settled on a negotiating team for possible seats at the American-brokered Russia-Ukraine peace talks. The president of the European Council announced the decision after an informal summit in Dublin on Friday: Britain, France, Germany, Italy and Poland, the E5 bloc, will represent Europe, alongside envoys from the Commission and the Council. The outcome defied calls from Washington, Kyiv and Moscow for a single European envoy. No negotiators have been named; the five states are likely to field national security advisers rather than heads of government, and it is still unclear who will speak for the institutions, in the account. The deal comes on the heels of the talks in Abu Dhabi, where European officials held separate discussions but were shut out of the core negotiations; the American envoys then met the Russian President in Moscow and the Ukrainian leader in Dublin, and announced that both sides had agreed to bring Europe into the next round. Moscow has not confirmed European participation, in the account. No date has been fixed for the new talks, but the Kremlin’s spokesman said on Friday they will happen fairly soon, probably in Abu Dhabi again, in the account.

 SubjectiveReuters — Spain’s right retains a firm poll lead despite Socialist gains, in three polls published on MondayMadrid, November 16. Spain’s conservative People’s Party and Vox would together win a parliamentary majority in the November 29 election, three opinion polls published on Monday showed, though Prime Minister S&aacute;nchez’s Socialists gained ground. The surveys are the first since last week’s campaign launch, which has focused on housing affordability, immigration, corruption and last month’s deadly train crash. A daily poll showed the Socialists rising to 30.3 percent from 29.9 percent, exceeding the 30 percent mark for the first time in that poll since the 2023 election; the People’s Party, on 31.5 percent, and Vox, on 18 percent, would together win more than 190 seats in the 350-seat lower house, a majority. A second poll projected 201 to 205 seats for the two parties combined, and 102 to 104 for the Socialists, whose support rose half a percentage point to 26.1 percent. A third poll showed Socialist support up one percentage point from a week earlier to 26.9 percent, with the right bloc winning 194 seats to the Socialists’ 109. The state poll remained a major outlier: last week it projected 134 to 143 seats for the Socialists against 155 to 171 for the People’s Party and Vox combined, suggesting the Prime Minister could retain power through a broad left-wing coalition.

 SubjectiveDem&oacute;crata — the survey of November 16: both large parties rise, Vox loses four seats, and the right maintains the majorityThe start of the November 29 campaign reinforces the two major parties without altering the parliamentary majority the study attributes to the People’s Party and Vox. The fourth wave of the study, with fieldwork carried out between November 10 and 13 and published on November 16, places the Conservatives at 31.5 percent of the votes and the Socialists at 26.9 percent. The People’s Party gains 1.7 points and two seats, to 128; the Socialists recover one point and three representatives, to 109; Vox drops from 19.9 percent to 19.0 percent and from 70 to 66 seats. The two right parties together stand at 194 seats, against 176 needed for a majority.

 SubjectiveParticle News — the fifth Saturday at 106,000, the police bill to the Senate, and a strike on TuesdayThe nationwide demonstrations ran for a fifth Saturday in a row on November 14 and the Interior Ministry put turnout at about 106,000 people, including roughly 24,000 in Paris, while organisers gave higher estimates.
